Senses.Explanation: To stick out the tongue is an ordinary bodily action that Zen records place inside public encounters. After Baizhang Huaihai recounts that Mazu Daoyi's shout left him deaf for three days, Huangbo Xiyun sticks out his tongue without intending to; three records preserve that one encounter. Nanyuan Daoming deliberately gives the gesture when asked for one word, then says he will answer when he has the broad, long tongue-mark. The official Yang Danian sticks out his tongue and calls Shishuang Chuyuan a true dragon-elephant after their exchange. Fengqi Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue when asked what purpose his appearance as abbot serves, then says, 'Just this—what else is there?' Hanyue Fazang uses the gesture after an unnamed interlocutor says he has caught him, while Linji Yixuan does it after Puhua rebukes his distinction between coarse and fine. The records therefore show both reaction and deliberate answer without assigning one fixed emotion or meaning to every occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: To become a buddha and become a patriarch names a paired ambition. In a case raised by Dahui Zonggao, Linji Yixuan says that his conduct makes the attendant become a buddha and a patriarch. Huanglong Huinan calls it a stairway, while Ying’an Tanhua and Chushi Fanqi call the ambition a mistaken use of mind or delusion. Other speakers use it as a promise or condition, so no single appraisal governs the pair.

Senses.Explanation: To accomplish the Way is to awaken as a buddha or complete the Way. Yongming Yanshou’s compiled treatise links it to cultivating the one mind; Shakyamuni biographies place it at the morning star; Baizhang Huaihai names the conventional eight-aspect account while subjecting such conceptual traces to scrutiny. The Zen Buddha remains visible in the term’s attested use: the biographies lead from accomplishment to the entrusted treasury of the true teaching, while Baizhang refuses to let a hagiographic sequence become a final conceptual possession.

Senses.Explanation: The Buddha’s awakening day is the annual occasion named awakening day. A colophon dates itself by that observance, and Konggu Daocheng ascends the hall on the World-Honored One’s awakening day. Konggu does not merely mark a date: his address immediately takes up the Buddha seeing the star, Yunmen’s criticism, the birth proclamation, and later claims about long-completed buddhahood.

Senses.Explanation: The furnace and bellows image names the testing heat of a teaching place or severe handling. Fachang Yiyu contrasts the furnace with dull iron; Feiyin Tongrong opens the furnace and asks who will not avoid its fire; Ying'an Tanhua calls experienced guides a furnace and proper tongs. Yune Xiyue uses it in an opening-the-furnace encounter, and Chaozong Tongren recalls Miyun Yuanwu's severe furnace in transmission incense. The isolated verse witness remains compiler-narrated because its local heading does not securely name the poet.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula “chasing the clod.” In the corpus it belongs to a recurrent animal comparison: “the lion bites the person; the hound chases the clod.” The phrase appears as an appraisal after exchanges and in admonitions such as “you must be a lion that bites the person; do not imitate the hound chasing the clod.” Related forms call people “mad dogs chasing the clod” and say “chasing the clod and tracking the scent does not yet make a good dog.” The hound and mad-dog variants share one literal image and one corpus use; they are not separate senses.
